extracted.intended_audience: general public; science communicators; researchers, journals and publishers interested in public engagement
extracted.subtask_short: explaining peer review to the public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for communicating the role, value and limits of scholarly peer review to non-specialist audiences, and for institutions/publishers to open up the workings of the process. Includes principles for public guides, outreach and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present peer review as scrutiny (not proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain peer review to the public as a tool that means a claim has been 'scrutinized' rather than proven true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the phrase and concept that 'peer reviewed means scrutinized' to set realistic expectations about what peer review conveys about a finding's status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equating peer review with absolute truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not promote false certainties by implying that peer review means a result is definitively true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that peer review can fail and that being peer reviewed is a helpful rule of thumb, not an infallible stamp of truth; provide caveats so the public does not over-interpret review as final correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations and failures openly
rubrics_metrics.description: Be transparent about the system's shortcomings, including that fraud, bias and misconduct sometimes get through peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss examples and recognize mistakes, bias and delays as real phenomena so audiences can accept fallibility while still valuing the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize that a single paper is not the end of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate that one peer-reviewed paper is only part of an ongoing scientific conversation where conflicting views coexist and compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage audiences to see evidence-building as cumulative and iterative rather than concluding from a single study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familiar analogies to explain how peer review works
rubrics_metrics.description: Help public understanding by comparing peer review to more familiar systems (the text uses the criminal justice system analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies (e.g., criminal justice: imperfect but valuable) can make abstract ideas about scrutiny, fallibility and collective deliberation easier to grasp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convene stakeholders to share the workings of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Research institutions, journals, publishers and others should actively explain and open up the peer review process to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sense about Science convened working groups and recommended greater effort by these stakeholders; collaboration across organizations (publishers, learned societies, funders) is advised to produce credible public-facing explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce accessible public-facing guides and outreach activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Create clear guides, surveys, workshops and events to raise awareness of the role of evidence and the mechanics of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the 'I don't know what to believe' public guide, Peer Review Week, surveys and workshops; use written guides plus events to both inform and debate challenges to the system.
